source: Sinha & Kapur (2021) When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure (Rev. Educ. Res. 91(5))
finding: Main meta-analysis of problem-solving-then-instruction (PS-I) versus instruction-then-problem-solving (I-PS). PS-I wins for conceptual knowledge and transfer. No gain for procedural knowledge. Gain is larger when the design follows productive failure (PF) principles.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Hedges g = 0.36 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.51) for conceptual understanding and transfer. A publication-bias-corrected figure of about 0.87 is reported in secondary summaries. Sample mix: 45% secondary, 37% undergraduate, 15% primary; 43% N. America, 26% Europe, 28% Asia. Read via abstract text in a search result plus the phys.org summary; full PDF was blocked (403).
limits: Full paper not read. The 0.87 figure appears only in secondary sources and the Chinese-language abstract; g=0.36 is the cleaner number. Primary-school students and procedural tasks showed no benefit. Excludes humanities and social-science problems.
agent_relevance: Base rate for the 'attempt first, instruct after' idea: a moderate effect (g about 0.36), not a universal one. Expect gains on concept and transfer, not on routine procedure.

source: phys.org (2021) Those who fail productively are all the wiser (ETH press summary of Sinha & Kapur 2021)
finding: Press summary of the meta-analysis plus a field test. States the age boundary (secondary and undergraduate gain more than primary) and reports a linear algebra course test.
numbers: 53 studies, 166 comparisons. Linear algebra course about 650 students; about 60% did the voluntary pre-lecture problems; historic pass rate about 55%; success rate among those who engaged was about 20% higher (relative). No effect size in the article.
limits: Press piece, not a paper. Contains no g values. 'Twice as efficient as a year of good teaching' is a press claim, not a finding.
agent_relevance: Do not cite press multipliers. Use only the age boundary: weak domain knowledge and weak analytic reasoning in the learner reduce the gain.

source: Loibl, Roll & Rummel (2017) Towards a theory of when and how problem solving followed by instruction supports learning (Educ. Psychol. Rev.)
finding: Review that maps PS-I designs to outcomes. PS-I helps only if the instruction phase uses contrasting cases or builds on student solutions. Proposes three mechanisms: activate prior knowledge, make students aware of knowledge gaps, recognise deep features.
numbers: Effect sizes across studies range from d = 1.12 down to d = -0.54 (range quoted in Sinha et al. 2019, see b12). Only the abstract page was read here.
quote: PS-I fosters learning only if specific design features (namely contrasting cases or building instruction on student solutions) are implemented
limits: Only abstract read. Narrative review, not a pooled estimate. Theory is built post hoc from the studies.
agent_relevance: The attempt alone is not the active ingredient. The lesson step must reuse the agent's own failed attempts (compare and contrast). This supports storing failed attempts and reading the lesson against them.

source: Darabi, Arrington, Sayilir (2018) Learning from failure: a meta-analysis of the empirical studies (ETR&D)
finding: Earlier, smaller meta-analysis. Learning from failure gives a moderately positive effect. Grade level, domain and study duration were not significant moderators, though each showed medium effects.
numbers: 187 publications screened, 62 relevant, only 12 experimental with usable statistics. Overall effect: 'moderately positive'. Covers only productive failure and failure-driven memory.
limits: Abstract page only. Tiny evidence base (12 studies) and mixes different 'failure' designs. Superseded in size by b01.
agent_relevance: Even the early evidence base was thin. Treat any single failure-based tactic as one hypothesis to test in our own ablation, not a settled gain.

source: Nachtigall, Serova & Rummel (2020) When failure fails to be productive: PF beyond STEM (Instr. Sci. 48)
finding: Two quasi-experiments with 10th graders on social-science research methods (experimental design). Productive failure did not beat direct instruction. In study 1, direct instruction was clearly better. In study 2 there was no difference (Bayes factor favoured the null).
numbers: Study 1 N=212 (PF 121, DI 91). Total posttest PF 10.97 (SD 5.22) vs DI 13.88 (SD 3.99), F(1,209)=27.46, partial eta2=.12. Transfer items PF 5.96 vs DI 8.04 (scale 0-16). Multilevel beta=-3.07, p<.001. Study 2 N=152 (PF 80, DI 72): F(1,148)=0.32, p=.57, partial eta2=.002; BF10=0.23. Only 24% (study 1) and 9% (study 2) of PF students solved a familiar posttest task canonically vs 48% and 18% of DI.
quote: PF students did not outperform DI students on learning social science research methods.
limits: Quasi-experimental, assigned by class (11 and 7 clusters). Group work. Domain is knowledge ABOUT science. Authors list conjectures only.
agent_relevance: Clean failed replication in a non-STEM, ill-structured domain. Do not assume an attempt-first step helps on every task type. Needs a switch by task type.

source: Nachtigall, Serova & Rummel (2020), mechanism analysis
finding: Why it failed, from the process data. PF students did not notice their failure. After the attempt they felt MORE competent than DI students, and only after instruction did they feel less competent. Quality, not quantity, of their first attempts predicted learning.
numbers: Perceived competence after phase 1: PF 3.53 vs DI 3.09, F(1,209)=18.93, partial eta2=.08. After phase 2: PF 3.02 vs DI 3.92, partial eta2=.23. Solution quality vs posttest r=.33 (individual), r=.55 (group, n=44). Solution quantity vs posttest r=.11 (ns). Perceived competence after phase 1 vs posttest r=.03.
limits: Correlational. Self-reports on a 1-5 scale. Authors suggest the IKEA effect (overvaluing own work) and missing feedback; untested.
agent_relevance: Key mechanism for our agent: an attempt only helps if the attempt visibly fails against some check. Without feedback the agent, like the students, can stay overconfident. Pair attempt with an executable or external check (links to Calibration subfield).

source: Loibl & Leuders (2025, online 2024) Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication (Instr. Sci. 53)
finding: Conceptual replication of Loibl & Rummel (2014) with Bayesian reasoning. No effect of PS-I vs I-PS and no effect of building on typical student solutions. Cause: students did not explore.
numbers: N=75, 2x2 design. Conceptual knowledge, order of phases: F(1,71)=0.84, partial eta2 about .01 (ns). Procedural, order: F(1,71)=0.04, p=.84. 31 of 38 students in PS-I generated only ONE solution attempt, versus a mean of 4.13 (SD 1.35) in the original study. Group means about 2.4 vs 2.3 points on a short scale.
quote: students merely activated their prior knowledge on probabilities without exploring the problem-solving space
limits: Single topic. Authors note power was adequate for the original effect size but maybe not a smaller one. Mismatch between generated and taught solutions.
agent_relevance: Breadth of attempts is the active variable. A single attempt gives no lesson. Our loop should force several different attempts before the lesson, not one.

source: Braas, Hartmann, Hoogerheide, Rummel & van Gog (2025) When is observing failure productive? Solution diversity in vicarious failure (Instr. Sci. 53)
finding: Four conditions: own productive failure, vicarious failure with high-diversity attempts, vicarious failure with low-diversity attempts, direct instruction. Watching a high-diversity set of failed attempts did as well as failing yourself, and beat direct instruction. The standard PF-over-DI effect did NOT replicate in this sample.
numbers: N=152 secondary students. Conceptual ANCOVA F(3,140)=3.078, p=.030, partial eta2=.062. VF-high vs VF-low d=0.644 (p=.014); VF-high vs DI d=0.648 (p=.010); VF-high vs PF d=0.292 (ns); PF vs DI p=.170, d=0.294 (ns); VF-low vs DI d=0.05.
quote: students' activation of prior knowledge is more critical than whether they experience failure first hand
limits: Math topic with four canonical components. Failure examples were designed to cover all components. PF vs DI under-powered for d near 0.3.
agent_relevance: The agent may not need to fail itself. A diverse set of other attempts (sampled solutions, other agents' wrong answers) can serve as the pre-lesson. Diversity of the failed set matters more than ownership.

source: Mazziotti, Rummel, Deiglmayr & Loibl (2019) Probing boundary conditions of PF and the role of young students' collaboration (npj Sci. Learn. 4:2)
finding: Fifth graders (math). No PF advantage over direct instruction, and no difference between collaborative and individual work. Age is a boundary condition.
numbers: N=228, 9 classes, 3 schools. Posttest (max 18): PF-collab 10.31 (SD 2.45), PF-individual 10.80, DI-collab 10.50, DI-individual 11.28. Timing: F(1,224)=1.01, p=.32, partial eta2=.005. Social form: F(1,224)=3.36, p=.06. Solution ideas about 4.1 to 4.5 per unit. Posttest alpha=.54.
limits: Quasi-experimental by class. Weak test reliability (alpha .54). Young children may lack executive control and persistence.
agent_relevance: Learner capability gates the effect. For a weak solver, an open attempt yields few diverse attempts and little benefit. Match the open-attempt step to the model's competence.

source: Baumgartner, Daguati, Trninic, Akveld, Caspar, Hungerbuhler & Kapur (2025) Problem-solving before instruction for linear algebra in university mathematics (Instr. Sci. 53)
finding: Four-year design-based study in a real university course. Voluntary preparatory problems before lectures raised exam grades each year versus an aggregate of earlier cohorts.
numbers: Exam grade effect vs baseline: d=0.38, 0.59, 0.28, 0.54 for years 1-4 (range d 0.28 to 0.59). Passing rate d between 0.21 and 0.42; year 1 +14% passing, one year +10%. Up to 16% of exam variance explained by participation. Mean grade +0.42 points (8.4%) in year 1.
quote: effect sizes between Cohen's d=0.28 and d=0.59
limits: No control group; cohort comparison; participation was voluntary so self-selection is possible. Authors refuse causal claims about components.
agent_relevance: Real-world effect sizes are in the same range as the meta-analysis (g about 0.36) and survive in a messy setting. Still weak evidence about mechanism.

source: Sinha, Kapur, West, Catasta, Hauswirth & Trninic (2019) Impact of explicit failure and success-driven preparatory activities on learning (CogSci 41)
finding: Classroom test of scaffolds in the problem phase. Scaffolds that push students toward failure (problematizing) beat scaffolds that push toward success (structuring), for conceptual understanding. Gains depend on topic and posttest type.
numbers: N=221. Topic SC non-isomorphic conceptual: chi2(3)=11.73, p=.008, d=0.409; isomorphic: chi2(3)=1.37, p=.712 (ns). Topic AQ: non-isomorphic chi2(3)=10.84, p=.012, d=0.387; isomorphic chi2(3)=20.16, p=.0001, d=0.586. Equivalence tests: 24 of 28 pairs equivalent for some outcomes.
limits: Conference paper; mixed omnibus results; topic-dependent. Authors flag that students may not be ready for explicit structuring on difficult topics.
agent_relevance: Hints that only help the model succeed early may remove the useful failure. When a lesson is added, delay the hint that gives away the method.

source: Sinha, Kapur et al. (2019) CogSci 41, reference to Loibl et al. 2017 spread
finding: Reports that effect sizes across PS-I studies vary widely, with some negative.
numbers: Cohen's d from 1.12 down to -0.54 across PS-I studies (citing Loibl et al., 2017).
quote: considerable variation in effect sizes (Cohen's d = 1.12 - 0.54)
limits: Second-hand citation; the minus sign appears garbled in extraction, read as range from -0.54 to 1.12.
agent_relevance: The sign of the effect depends on design details. Any adoption in the schema must be tested per task, with a null result as a live outcome.

source: Authors not confirmed (2023) Prior math achievement and inventive production predict learning from productive failure (npj Sci. Learn.)
finding: Two quasi-experiments in two Singapore schools with very different prior math. Number of solution methods invented (inventive production) was much more associated with learning than prior achievement. Prior achievement did not predict learning once production was in the model.
numbers: Schools differed hugely in PSLE score (d=5.34 and 2.49; math grade d=2.12 and 1.23) but differed little in number of methods generated (ratio topic d=0.48; variance topic d=0.03). Number of solutions vs posttest F(1,107)=62.6, p<.001 and F(1,100)=105.5, p<.001; prior PSLE math effect ns in the second study (F=0.001).
limits: Author list not recorded. Quasi-experimental. Counting solutions is a crude proxy.
agent_relevance: Diversity of attempts is a stronger predictor than ability. So for the agent, count and vary distinct attempts as a cheap proxy for readiness for the lesson.

source: Kapur (2012) Productive failure in learning the concept of variance (Instr. Sci. 40)
finding: Original 9th-grade variance study (Singapore). PF students generated many formulas but never reached the canonical one. After instruction they beat DI students on conceptual understanding and transfer, with equal procedural fluency.
numbers: 140 ninth-grade students (from the 2010 conference version of the same study). Full statistics were not accessible; abstract only.
quote: PF students significantly outperformed DI students on conceptual understanding and transfer without compromising procedural fluency.
limits: Abstract page only. Single lab group. Compare and contrast consolidation by teacher.
agent_relevance: The founding result: accuracy on procedure does not drop, concept and transfer rise. Matches the schema memory idea 'lessons after the first attempt'.

source: Kapur (2009) Productive failure in mathematical problem solving (Instr. Sci. 38)
finding: Quasi-experiment on rate and speed with 7th graders. PF students failed to solve problems but beat lecture-and-practice students on well-structured and higher-order problems, and on a later relative-speed task not taught.
numbers: N=75 seventh graders, 2-week unit. PF groups reported low confidence in their solutions (this contrasts with the German study b06, where PF students were over-confident).
limits: Abstract only. Intact classes, one school, one teacher effect risk.
agent_relevance: Note the confidence difference: in the Singapore studies students knew they had failed; in the German social-science study they did not. Awareness of failure may be the moderator.

source: Puech, Macina, Chatain, Sachan & Kapur (2025; arXiv 2410.03781) Towards the pedagogical steering of LLMs for tutoring: a case study with modeling productive failure (Findings of ACL 2025)
finding: StratL steers an LLM tutor along a productive failure plan using a transition graph of tutoring intents. Plain prompting with a written description of the strategy failed to keep the model on the PF plan. The tutor was tested with simulated students and with real students.
numbers: Field study N=17 ninth graders in Singapore, 15 minutes each, two problems. StratL tutor elicited on average 2.6 student solution methods on the invention problem vs baseline that failed to elicit several (p=.05). PF score higher with StratL (p=.046 on Consistency). Student-state tracing micro F1=0.77. Students rated the StratL tutor less helpful (1.20 vs 2.00 of 3 on Consistency). 15-problem PF dataset released.
quote: providing a natural language description of the tutoring strategy to follow ... does not yield satisfactory results
limits: Tiny sample. Measures PF fidelity (number of solution methods), NOT learning gain. No posttest. Tutor persona only.
agent_relevance: Shows a language model's default is to reveal the answer. Holding back needs a structured state machine, not a prompt sentence. Same lesson for our schema: attempt-first must be enforced by states and operators.

source: Puech et al. (2025), simulated-student preliminary study
finding: Ablation of tutor versions with simulated students. Letting the LLM choose the intent from a natural-language strategy description (V4) beat plain LLM (V2) but not the handcrafted intent selection (V1). A version that never hints (V3) scores high on the PF score by construction but elicits few methods (mean 1.34).
numbers: V3 average 1.34 solution methods, lower than V1. Student-state tracing with written justification beat no justification; keeping only the last 3 dialog pairs was worse than the full history.
limits: Simulated students are LLMs. The PF score can be gamed by a tutor that never helps.
agent_relevance: Two warnings: (1) a rule 'never reveal' trivially scores well on a naive metric. (2) Full history for state tracing beats truncated history.

source: Suriyaarachchi, Denny & Nanayakkara (2025; arXiv 2411.11227) Productive failure as a design paradigm for introductory Python (SIGCSE TS 2025)
finding: Small lab study in programming. No difference right after the activity. Two weeks later, direct-instruction students more often failed to reproduce the solution. Heart-rate data suggested PF students showed a larger drop in cognitive load after instruction.
numbers: 20 participants enrolled, 16 questionnaires analysed (DI n=9, PF n=7). 3 of 9 DI students failed the delayed task; all PF students kept their earlier success. 9 of 16 preferred PF. No inferential statistics reported.
limits: Very small, descriptive, no tests. Wearable heart-rate measure is a weak proxy for load. Not an LLM study (programming domain only).
agent_relevance: Weak support for retention benefit in code. Only a hypothesis; our own coding benchmarks should test it.

source: Rotter, Benazet i Montobbio & Hernandez-Leo (2026; arXiv 2605.15850) Access timing as scaffolding: an RL approach to GenAI in education
finding: A reinforcement-learning policy decides when students may use a generative AI, with reward shaped by productive failure (do not help too early, help after struggle, penalise long unaided failure). RL timing beat always-on AI and matched never-AI on test scores.
numbers: N=105 university students (Always n=36, RL n=37, Never n=32). Posttest RL vs Always t(71)=2.51, p=.014, d=0.59. RL vs Never t(67)=-0.30, p=.762, d=-0.07. Metacognitive accuracy RL vs Always d=0.54 (p=.023); RL vs Never d=0.07 (ns). Self-reported metacognitive awareness: no difference. Policy trained on a simulated student (Bayesian knowledge tracing) with parameters from a pilot of n=9.
limits: Preprint under review. Gender imbalance across conditions. Nothing shows the benefit comes specifically from the productive-failure reward term rather than from any delay. 'Never use AI' was not worse, so timing mostly avoided harm.
agent_relevance: The only found study linking PF to AI-assistance timing. Evidence that a wait-then-help order beats instant help; but it does not beat no help.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics (PNAS 122)
finding: Large field experiment. Unrestricted GPT-4 access improved practice scores but lowered later unassisted exam scores; a tutor version that gave hints and not answers removed the harm. This is the 'unproductive success' pattern, though the paper is not a PF test.
numbers: About 1,000 high school students in Turkey. Practice improvement 48% (GPT Base) and 127% (GPT Tutor). Exam: GPT Base 17% worse than control; GPT Tutor about equal to control. Figures from search-result summary only.
limits: NOT OPENED: full text blocked (403). Numbers taken from secondary summaries. One country, one subject.
agent_relevance: Strong LLM-era evidence that showing the answer immediately removes the learning. For an agent, the analogue is skipping the attempt: a quick correct answer is not the same as a retained method.

source: Nachtigall et al. (2020), discussion of earlier null and negative PS-I results
finding: Lists earlier studies outside STEM or outside the standard PF design that found no effect or a negative effect of problem solving before instruction, and offers a conjecture that PF suits knowledge OF a domain more than knowledge ABOUT how the domain works.
numbers: Table 2 of the paper lists studies such as Glogger-Frey et al. 2015 (negative effect), Chase & Klahr 2017 (no advantage), Matlen & Klahr, Kant et al. 2017, Tam 2017, Marei et al. 2017. Details not extracted here.
quote: PF ... may rather apply to students' acquisition of knowledge of science than ... knowledge about science
limits: Hypothesis only; no direct test. I read the discussion text, not the cited primary papers.
agent_relevance: Task-type split to test: concept tasks (what is it, why does the rule work) versus method-about-method tasks. May belong in a task-type switch for O-level operators.

source: Nachtigall et al. (2020), design checks
finding: The design met the usual PF conditions yet the effect still failed. This rules out 'bad implementation' as the easy explanation.
numbers: Missing typical errors in PF student solutions: pretest absent in 93%, systematic variation of variables violated in 82%, control variable not named in 64%, no control group in 64%. Best attempt used 7 canonical principles in only 2 groups. Study 2: collaborative task score PF 3.18 vs DI 4.57 of 8; transfer scale PF vs DI F(1,149)=0.09, p=.77.
limits: Same single research team and domain.
agent_relevance: Even with typical errors present and taught against, no gain. So the contrast step alone is not sufficient; the learner must also see the attempt as failed.

source: Loibl & Leuders (2025), original-versus-replication comparison
finding: Authors ask whether the original effect is general or context-bound. They rule out low power as the main reason and point to the learning process: the data sets did not make students see that their prior method fails.
numbers: Original: about 4 attempts per student. Replication: 31 of 38 produced a single attempt used on all three cases. Differences in data presentation (graph plus numbers) may have removed the typical wrong attempts.
limits: Post hoc explanation, no manipulation of the presentation.
agent_relevance: The problem has to be built so that the obvious method visibly fails (a designed impasse). For an agent: select or construct test cases that break the first plausible method (links to Cognitive conflict and impasse).

source: Baumgartner et al. (2025), alignment with the meta-analysis
finding: Authors note that their year-1 effect (d=0.38) lines up with the meta-analytic Hedges g=0.36 for conceptual understanding and transfer, which suggests a stable typical size of about a third of a standard deviation.
numbers: d=0.38 in year 1 against g=0.36 in the meta-analysis.
quote: in line with the effect size found by Sinha and Kapur (2021) of Hedge's g=0.36
limits: Consistency of two numbers, not a test.
agent_relevance: Plan sample sizes in our benchmark with an expected effect near 0.3 SD; small tests will be underpowered, as in b08 and b07.

source: Mazziotti et al. (2019), authors' explanation of the null
finding: Authors describe an 'experimental dilemma': the standard PF problem is too hard for young children, while problems suited to them give older students no real failure. Process data inside the PF group: more constructive talk went with more solution ideas and higher posttest scores.
numbers: Dyad constructive utterances vs solution ideas r(32)=.411, p=.008. Individual relative constructive utterances vs posttest r(66)=.233, p=.028. Solution quality in PF was not tied to extra gains over DI.
limits: Correlational on one sample; coding scheme ICAP may be too coarse.
agent_relevance: Difficulty must be tuned to the learner. An agent loop needs a difficulty check: if the problem cannot be partly solved, the attempt is wasted.

source: Sinha et al. (2019) CogSci, person-centred analysis and conclusions
finding: Clusters of students differ on incoming traits. Awareness of knowledge gaps and germane load had small positive links to posttest scores. Authors argue that quick easy success can be insufficiently disruptive and make students inattentive during instruction.
numbers: Person-centred omnibus effects up to d=0.647 (AQ, isomorphic, chi2(7)=27.16, p=.0003). Awareness of knowledge gaps vs isomorphic and non-isomorphic scores beta=.112 and .172*. High-cluster students had lower extraneous load.
limits: Conference paper; many comparisons; betas small.
agent_relevance: The 'success is not always good' idea: a first answer that works too easily may cause the agent (and student) to skim the lesson.

source: Rotter et al. (2026), PF-inspired reward design
finding: Concrete, copyable form of PF as a policy: (1) discourage giving extra help too early, (2) promote help after productive struggle, (3) penalise prolonged or excessive failure. Paper states no earlier study had tested PF with generative AI.
numbers: Reward terms only; hyperparameters in supplement (not read). BKT agent trained in simulation; pilots n=9 and n=7.
limits: The claim 'no studies to date' was made by the authors and not checked by me. Design choices not ablated.
agent_relevance: A usable rule for the agent controller: allow N attempts, give help only after a stall, cap total failure. Fits a state-machine escalation (attempt, check, lesson).

source: Puech et al. (2025), student comments and risks
finding: The PF tutor frustrated students and was rated less helpful than the baseline. A tracing error produced a contradictory instruction, quoted by a student: the AI kept asking to check an answer that was correct.
numbers: Helpfulness (of 3): StratL 1.20 vs baseline 2.00 on Consistency; 2.67 vs 2.80 on Country. Coherence 1.80 vs 2.25. None significant.
quote: The AI keeps on asking me to check my answer although it was correct
limits: Tiny N, 3-point scale.
agent_relevance: Holding back has a cost in perceived usefulness; state-tracing errors turn it into an annoying loop. Needs a loop breaker (G-level guardrail on repeated checks).
